name: Theorem
section: Read the claim before choosing a method
quick: A mathematical statement established by proof.
definition: A theorem includes its domain and hypotheses as well as its conclusion. A proof must cover every case the statement promises.
example: “For every integer n, if n is even then its square is even” includes an integer-domain restriction.
confusion: Examples illustrate a universal theorem but do not prove all cases.

name: Direct proof
section: Read the claim before choosing a method
quick: Assume the hypotheses and deduce the conclusion.
definition: For an implication about every x in a domain, choose x arbitrarily, assume the stated hypothesis, and reason forward with definitions and established facts.
example: If $n=2k$ with integer k, then $n^2=2(2k^2)$ is even.
confusion: Do not assume the conclusion you are trying to establish.

name: Hypothesis
section: Read the claim before choosing a method
quick: An assumption supplied by a claim.
definition: In an if-then statement, the “if” conditions are available in the proof; the “then” statement is the conclusion to establish.
example: In “if n is positive and even,” both properties may be used.
confusion: A condition appearing only in the conclusion is not yet available.

name: Integral value
definition: Here integral means belonging to the integers, not an operation from calculus. A witness in a divisibility equation or an even/odd representation must be an integer.
confusion: An expression looking like twice something is not proof of evenness unless that something is an integer.

name: Even and odd integers
quick: Even integers are 2k; odd integers are 2k+1, with integer k.
definition: These two forms partition the integers, including negative values and zero. The integer witness is part of each definition.
confusion: Allowing a real witness would destroy the distinction.

name: Integer linear combination
quick: A sum of integer multiples of specified integers.
definition: For integers a,b,r,s, the expression $ra+sb$ is an integer linear combination of a and b. A common divisor of a,b divides every such combination.
confusion: Integer coefficients are essential to the divisibility conclusion.

name: Closure under an operation
quick: Allowed inputs always produce an output in the same set.
definition: To prove closure, choose arbitrary inputs in the set and check every defining property of their result, including nonzero denominators.
example: Two rationals $a/b,c/d$ sum to $(ad+bc)/(bd)$ with nonzero integer denominator.
confusion: Division of integers is not generally integer-valued; closure depends on the operation.

name: Parity
quick: Whether an integer is even or odd.
definition: Parity classifies integers into the even and odd cases. A proof by parity must include both when no hypothesis rules one out.
example: Consecutive integers have opposite parity, so their product is even.
confusion: Parity is not an exhaustive classification of arbitrary real numbers.

name: Proof by cases
quick: Cover all allowed possibilities and prove the conclusion in each.
definition: The cases must be exhaustive: every input belongs to at least one. Overlap is allowed, but an omitted case leaves the proof incomplete.
example: To show $n(n+1)$ even, split into even n and odd n.
confusion: Positive and negative cases omit zero when the domain is all reals.

name: Constructive existence
quick: Build a witness and verify all required properties.
definition: An existence proof is constructive when it supplies a way to obtain the promised object. Check its domain as well as its defining equations or inequalities.
confusion: The construction of a real midpoint does not supply an integer between consecutive integers.

name: Circular reasoning
quick: Using the desired conclusion as an assumption in its own proof.
definition: A chain of calculations proves a theorem only if it starts from permitted assumptions. Working backward can aid discovery but the finished proof needs justified forward steps or reversible equivalences.
example: Assuming every even square has an even root cannot prove that same claim.
confusion: A correct algebraic consequence of the desired result does not necessarily imply the result.
